title: Part 2, Chapter 20
paragraphs: Giving an account of the wedding of Camacho the rich, together with the incident of Basilio the poor

Scarcely had fair Aurora given bright Phœbus time to dry the liquid pearls upon her golden locks with the heat of his fervent rays, when Don Quixote, shaking sloth from his limbs, sprang to his feet and called to his squire Sancho, who was still snoring. Seeing this, Don Quixote, before rousing him, addressed him thus: "Happy you, above all the dwellers on the face of the earth, who, without envying or being envied, sleep with a tranquil mind, and whom neither enchanters persecute nor enchantments frighten. Sleep, I say, and will say a hundred times, with no jealous thoughts of your mistress to make you keep ceaseless vigils, and no cares about how to pay the debts you owe or find tomorrow's food for yourself and your needy little family to interfere with your rest. Ambition does not break your rest, nor does this world's empty pomp disturb you; the utmost reach of your anxiety is to provide for your ass, since upon my shoulders you have laid the support of yourself, the counterweight and burden that nature and custom have imposed on masters. The servant sleeps, and the master lies awake thinking how to feed him, advance him, and reward him. The distress of seeing the sky turn brazen and withhold its needful moisture from the earth is felt not by the servant but by the master, who in times of scarcity and famine must support the one who served him in times of plenty and abundance."

To all this Sancho made no reply, because he was asleep; nor would he have wakened up so soon as he did, had not Don Quixote brought him round with the butt of his lance. He woke at last, drowsy and lazy, and casting his eyes about in every direction, observed, "From the direction of that arcade comes, if I'm not mistaken, a steam and a smell a great deal more like fried rashers than galingale or thyme. A wedding that begins with smells like that, by my faith, ought to be plentiful and unstinting."
"Enough, glutton," said Don Quixote. "Come, let us go and witness this wedding, and see what the rejected Basilio does."

"Let him do what he likes," Sancho returned. "If he weren't poor, he would marry Quiteria. To make a grand match for himself, and he without a farthing — is there nothing else? By my faith, señor, it's my view that the poor man should be content with what he can get, and not go looking for dainties at the bottom of the sea. I'll bet my arm that Camacho could bury Basilio in reales; and if that's so, as no doubt it is, what a fool Quiteria would be to refuse the fine dresses and jewels Camacho must have given her and will give her, and take instead Basilio's bar-throwing and swordplay. They won't give a pint of wine at the tavern for a good cast of the bar or a neat thrust of the sword. Talents and accomplishments that can't be turned into money — let Count Dirlos have them. But when such gifts fall on someone with hard cash, I only wish my own station in life were as becoming as those gifts. On a good foundation you can raise a good building, and the best foundation in the world is money."

"For God's sake, Sancho," said Don Quixote here, "stop that harangue. I believe that if you were allowed to go on with everything you start every other minute, you'd have no time left for eating or sleeping; you'd spend it all in talking."

"If your worship had a good memory," Sancho replied, "you'd remember the articles of our agreement before we set out from home this last time. One of them was that I was to be allowed to say all I liked, so long as it was not against my neighbour or your worship's authority; and so far, it seems to me, I have not broken that article."

"I remember no such article, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "and even if it were so, I want you to hold your tongue and come along, for the instruments we heard last night are already starting to enliven the valleys again, and no doubt the marriage will take place in the cool of the morning, and not in the heat of the afternoon."

Sancho did as his master told him, and putting the saddle on Rocinante and the pack-saddle on Dapple, they both mounted and at a leisurely pace entered the arcade. The first thing that met Sancho's eyes was a whole ox spitted on a whole elm tree, and in the fire over which it was to be roasted was burning a middling-sized mountain of faggots. Six stewpots that stood around the blaze had not been made in the ordinary mould of common pots: they were six half wine-jars, each fit to hold the contents of a slaughter-house — they swallowed whole sheep and hid them away inside without showing any more sign of them than if they were pigeons. Countless hares lay ready skinned, and plucked fowls hung from the trees ready for burial in the pots; numberless wildfowl and game of various sorts were suspended from the branches so the air might keep them cool. Sancho counted more than sixty wineskins of over six gallons each, all filled, as proved afterwards, with generous wines. There were also piles of the whitest bread, like the heaps of grain one sees on threshing-floors. There was a wall made of cheeses arranged like open brickwork, and two cauldrons full of oil, bigger than those of a dyer's shop, served for cooking fritters, which when fried were taken out with two mighty shovels and plunged into another cauldron of prepared honey standing close by. Of cooks and cook-maids there were more than fifty, all clean, brisk, and cheerful. In the capacious belly of the ox were a dozen soft little sucking-pigs, which, sewn up there, served to give it tenderness and flavour. The spices of various kinds did not seem to have been bought by the pound but by the quarter, and all lay open to view in a great chest. In short, all the preparations for the wedding were in rustic style, but plentiful enough to feed an army.

Sancho observed all, contemplated all, and everything won his heart. The first to captivate and take his fancy were the pots, out of which he would have very gladly helped himself to a moderate pipkinful; then the wineskins secured his affections; and lastly, the produce of the frying-pans — if indeed such imposing cauldrons can be called frying-pans. Unable to control himself or bear it any longer, he approached one of the busy cooks and civilly but hungrily begged permission to soak a scrap of bread in one of the pots. The cook answered, "Brother, this is not a day on which hunger is to have any sway, thanks to the rich Camacho. Get down and look about for a ladle and skim off a hen or two, and much good may they do you."
"I don't see one," said Sancho.

"Wait a moment," said the cook; "sinner that I am, how particular and shy you are!" So saying, he seized a bucket and plunging it into one of the half-jars took up three hens and a couple of geese, and said to Sancho, "Fall to, friend, and take the edge off your appetite with these skimmings until dinnertime comes."
"I have nothing to put them in," said Sancho.
"Well then," said the cook, "take spoon and all — for Camacho's wealth and happiness furnish everything."

While Sancho was thus occupied, Don Quixote was watching the entrance, at one end of the arcade, of some twelve peasants, all in holiday and gala dress, mounted on twelve beautiful mares with rich, handsome field trappings and a number of little bells attached to their petrals. Marshalled in regular order, they ran not one but several courses over the meadow, with jubilant shouts and cries of "Long live Camacho and Quiteria! He as rich as she is fair, and she the fairest on earth!"
Hearing this, Don Quixote said to himself, "It's easy to see these folk have never seen my Dulcinea del Toboso; for if they had, they'd be more moderate in their praises of this Quiteria of theirs."

Shortly after this, several bands of dancers of various sorts began to enter the arcade at different points, and among them one of sword-dancers, composed of some twenty-four lads of gallant and high-spirited bearing, dressed in the finest and whitest of linen, and with handkerchiefs embroidered in various colours with fine silk. One of those on the mares asked an active youth who led them whether any of the dancers had been wounded. "As yet, thank God, no one has been wounded," he said; "we are all safe and sound." And he at once began to execute complicated figures with the rest of his comrades, with so many turns and so great dexterity that, although Don Quixote was well used to seeing dances of the same kind, he thought he had never seen any so good as this. He also admired another that came in, made up of fair young maidens, none of whom seemed to be under fourteen or over eighteen, all dressed in green stuff, with their hair partly braided, partly flowing loose, but all of such bright gold as to vie with the sunbeams; and over their hair they wore garlands of jasmine, roses, amaranth, and honeysuckle. At their head were a venerable old man and an ancient dame, more brisk and active, however, than might have been expected from their years. The notes of a Zamora bagpipe accompanied them, and with modesty in their faces and in their eyes, and lightness in their feet, they looked the best dancers in the world.

Following these came an artistic dance of the sort they call "speaking dances." It was composed of eight nymphs in two files, with the god Cupid leading one and Interest the other — the former furnished with wings, bow, quiver, and arrows, the latter in a rich dress of gold and silk of various colours. The nymphs who followed Love bore their names written on white parchment in large letters on their backs. "Poetry" was the name of the first, "Wit" of the second, "Birth" of the third, and "Valour" of the fourth. Those who followed Interest were distinguished in the same way: the badge of the first announced "Liberality," that of the second "Largess," the third "Treasure," the fourth "Peaceful Possession." In front of them all came a wooden castle drawn by four wild men, all clad in ivy and hemp dyed green, and looking so lifelike that they nearly terrified Sancho. On the front of the castle and on each of the four sides of its frame it bore the inscription "Castle of Caution." Four skilful tabor and flute players accompanied them, and the dance having been opened, Cupid, after executing two figures, raised his eyes and bent his bow against a damsel who stood between the turrets of the castle, and addressed her thus:

I am the mighty God whose sway / Is potent over land and sea. / The heavens above us own me; nay, / The shades below acknowledge me. / I know not fear, I have my will, / Whate'er my whim or fancy be; / For me there's no impossible, / I order, bind, forbid, set free.

Having concluded the stanza he discharged an arrow at the top of the castle, and went back to his place. Interest then came forward and went through two more figures; and as soon as the tabors ceased, he said:

But mightier than Love am I, / Though Love it be that leads me on, / Than mine no lineage is more high, / Or older, underneath the sun. / To use me rightly few know how, / To act without me fewer still, / For I am Interest, and I vow / For evermore to do thy will.
Interest retired, and Poetry came forward; and when she had gone through her figures like the others, fixing her eyes on the damsel of the castle, she said:

With many a fanciful conceit, / Fair Lady, winsome Poesy / Her soul, an offering at thy feet, / Presents in sonnets unto thee. / If thou my homage wilt not scorn, / Thy fortune, watched by envious eyes, / On wings of poesy upborne / Shall be exalted to the skies.
Poetry withdrew, and on the side of Interest, Liberality advanced; and after going through her figures she said:

To give, while shunning each extreme, / The sparing hand, the over-free, / Therein consists, so wise men deem, / The virtue Liberality. / But thee, fair lady, to enrich, / Myself a prodigal I'll prove, / A vice not wholly shameful, which / May find its fair excuse in love.

In the same manner all the characters of the two bands advanced and retired, and each executed its figures and delivered its verses, some of them graceful, some burlesque; but Don Quixote's memory (although he had an excellent one) only carried away those just quoted. Then all mingled together, forming chains and breaking off again with graceful, unconstrained gaiety; and whenever Love passed in front of the castle he shot his arrows up at it, while Interest broke gilded pellets against it. At length, after they had danced a good while, Interest drew out a great purse, made of the skin of a large brindled cat and to all appearance full of money, and flung it at the castle; and with the force of the blow the boards fell asunder and tumbled down, leaving the damsel exposed and unprotected. Interest and the characters of his band advanced, and throwing a great chain of gold over her neck, pretended to lead her away captive. On seeing this, Love and his supporters made as though they would release her, the whole action being to the accompaniment of the tabors and in the form of a regular dance. The wild men made peace between them, and with great dexterity readjusted and fixed the boards of the castle, and the damsel once more ensconced herself within; and with this the dance wound up, to the great enjoyment of the spectators.

Don Quixote asked one of the nymphs who it was that had composed and arranged it. She replied that it was a beneficiary of the town who had a nice taste in devising things of the sort. "I would lay a wager," said Don Quixote, "that this same bachelor or beneficiary is a greater friend of Camacho's than of Basilio's, and that he is better at satire than at vespers; he has worked the accomplishments of Basilio and the riches of Camacho very neatly into the dance." Sancho Panza, who was listening to all this, exclaimed, "The king is my cock — I stick to Camacho." "It's easy to see you're a peasant, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and one of the sort that cry 'Long life to the conqueror.'"

"I don't know what sort I am," Sancho returned, "but I know very well that I'll never get such elegant skimmings off Basilio's pots as these I've got off Camacho's." And he showed him the bucketful of geese and hens, and seizing one began to eat with great gusto and appetite, saying, "A fig for the accomplishments of Basilio! As much as you have, so much are you worth; and as much as you are worth, so much do you have. As a grandmother of mine used to say, there are only two families in the world, the Haves and the Have-nots; and she stuck to the Haves. And to this day, Señor Don Quixote, people would sooner feel the pulse of 'Have' than of 'Know'; an ass covered with gold looks better than a horse with a pack-saddle. So once more I say I stick to Camacho — whose bountiful pot-skimmings are geese and hens, hares and rabbits — and not to Basilio's, whose, if any ever come to hand, or even to foot, will only be rinsings."

"Have you finished your harangue, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Of course I have finished it," Sancho replied, "because I see your worship takes offence at it; but if it weren't for that, there was work enough cut out for three days."
"God grant I may see you dumb before I die, Sancho," said Don Quixote.

"At the rate we are going," said Sancho, "I'll be chewing clay before your worship dies; and then, maybe, I'll be so dumb that I won't say a word until the end of the world, or at least till the day of judgment."

"Even if that happens, O Sancho," said Don Quixote, "your silence will never make up for all you have talked, are talking, and will talk all your life. Besides, it stands to reason that my death will come before yours; so I never expect to see you dumb, not even when you are drinking or sleeping, and that is the utmost I can say."

"In good faith, señor," Sancho replied, "there's no trusting that fleshless one — I mean Death — who devours the lamb as soon as the sheep, and, as I've heard our curate say, treads with equal foot upon the lofty towers of kings and the lowly huts of the poor. That lady is more mighty than dainty; she's in no way squeamish, she devours everything and is ready for everything, and fills her alforjas with people of all sorts, ages, and ranks. She's no reaper that sleeps out the noontide; at all hours she is reaping and cutting down the dry grass as well as the green. She never seems to chew, but bolts and swallows everything put before her, for she has a canine appetite that is never satisfied. And though she has no belly, she shows she has a dropsy and is thirsty to drink the lives of all who live, as one would drink a jug of cold water."

"Say no more, Sancho," said Don Quixote here; "don't try to better it, and risk a fall. In truth, what you have said about death in your rustic phrase is what a good preacher might have said. I tell you, Sancho, if you had discretion to match your native wit, you might take a pulpit in hand, and go about the world preaching fine sermons." "He preaches well who lives well," said Sancho, "and I know no more theology than that."
"Nor need you," said Don Quixote, "but I cannot conceive or make out how it is that, the fear of God being the beginning of wisdom, you, who are more afraid of a lizard than of Him, know so much."

"Pass judgment on your chivalries, señor," Sancho returned, "and don't set yourself up to judge of other men's fears or braveries, for I am as good a fearer of God as my neighbours. But leave me to finish off these skimmings, for all the rest is only idle talk that we'll be called to account for in the other world." And so saying, he began a fresh attack on the bucket with such hearty appetite that he aroused Don Quixote's, who no doubt would have helped him had he not been prevented by what must be told further on.
